common_name: Minnie Royal Cherry (Low-Chill Southern-Adapted Sweet Cherry)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun; Minnie Royal requires cross-pollination with its companion cultivar Royal Lee, which blooms simultaneously, and the two are almost always planted as an interlocking pair.

directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, always alongside its dedicated pollinizer Royal Lee, since neither cultivar reliably sets fruit on its own. Minnie Royal was bred specifically to satisfy fruit-bud chilling with only about 200 to 400 hours below 45 degrees Fahrenheit, opening sweet cherry growing to warm winter regions of the South that are far too mild for standard sweet cherry cultivars like Bing. Fruit is medium-sized, dark red, and ripens notably early, often well ahead of traditional sweet cherries, giving Gulf South and coastal growers a genuine shot at a home cherry crop. Because bloom is early, choose a site with good air drainage to reduce spring frost risk to the flowers.
sources: University of California Agriculture and Natural Resources

common_name: Royal Lee Cherry (Low-Chill Southern-Adapted Sweet Cherry)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun; Royal Lee requires cross-pollination with its companion cultivar Minnie Royal, which blooms at the same time, and the pair is planted together as interlocking pollinizers.

directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, and always pair with Minnie Royal for pollination, since Royal Lee will not set a usable crop alone. Like its companion, Royal Lee needs only around 200 to 400 chill hours, making it one of the few sweet cherries genuinely worth trying south of the traditional cherry belt, including parts of the Gulf Coast and lower South with mild winters. Fruit is firm, dark red, and ripens early in the season, roughly two weeks ahead of Bing, giving Southern growers a short but real cherry harvest window. Select a sunny, frost-protected planting site, since the trees' early bloom leaves flowers exposed to any late cold snaps.
sources: University of California Agriculture and Natural Resources

common_name: Royal Crimson Cherry (Self-Fruitful Low-Chill Sweet Cherry)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun; Royal Crimson is self-fruitful and does not require a second cherry tree, though planting near Minnie Royal or Royal Lee will improve fruit set.

directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; unlike most sweet cherries, Royal Crimson is self-fruitful, so a single tree can produce a crop without a separate pollinizer, though a nearby second tree improves yields. Bred from the same low-chill program that produced Minnie Royal and Royal Lee, Royal Crimson needs only about 200 to 300 chill hours, allowing it to fruit reliably in warm-winter Southern gardens where classic sweet cherries fail to break dormancy properly. The tree bears large, crimson-red, sweet fruit in early to mid-spring, ahead of most other sweet cherries. Because the crop ripens and blooms so early, choose a well-drained site with good air movement to protect flowers from late frost.
sources: University of California Agriculture and Natural Resources

common_name: AU-Cherry Plum (Auburn Disease-Resistant Southern Japanese Plum)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter or early spring in well-drained soil in full sun; AU-Cherry sets a good crop on its own but benefits from a second Japanese plum cultivar nearby, and is well suited to home orchards across the Southeast.

directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, siting a second plum cultivar nearby to boost fruit set even though AU-Cherry is largely self-fruitful. Released from Auburn University's fruit breeding program, AU-Cherry was selected specifically for the disease pressures of the humid Southeast, showing strong resistance to bacterial leaf spot and plum leaf scald that limit many older plum cultivars in the region. The small, dark red, cherry-like fruit ripens about two weeks after Methley with a sweet, juicy flavor good for fresh eating. Trees are noted for staying vigorous and productive for many years, making AU-Cherry a dependable long-term choice for Southern home orchards.
sources: Auburn University Alabama Agricultural Experiment Station

common_name: Excelsior Plum (Heirloom Low-Chill Japanese-American Hybrid Plum)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun; Excelsior needs a compatible plum cultivar such as Methley or Bruce nearby for cross-pollination, and its low chill requirement suits Gulf Coast and lower Southern gardens.

directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, and site a compatible plum cultivar such as Methley or Bruce within pollinating distance, since Excelsior needs a partner to set fruit reliably. Introduced from Florida nurseries over a century ago as one of the early hybrids between the Japanese plum and native American plum species, Excelsior has persisted as a heirloom home-orchard favorite in the Deep South thanks to a modest chill requirement of roughly 400 hours that suits mild Gulf Coast winters. Fruit ripens mid-season with deep wine-red skin and juicy yellow flesh, offering a good balance of sweetness and tartness for fresh eating. Give the upright tree room to spread and thin the crop if it sets heavily, since Excelsior can overbear on young trees.

common_name: Bryan Apricot (Texas Heat-Tolerant Home Orchard Apricot)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun; Bryan is self-fruitful and does not require a second apricot for pollination, and is among the more reliable apricot choices for Texas home orchards.

directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun; Bryan is self-fertile so a single tree can produce fruit without a pollinizer. A found seedling selection promoted by Texas A&M for its ability to bear fruit in the state's difficult apricot climate, Bryan is considered one of the more dependable apricots for Texas gardeners even though, like all apricots grown there, it does not crop every single year because of erratic late-winter warm spells followed by hard freezes. Fruit is medium-sized with the classic sweet-tart apricot flavor, good for fresh eating, preserves, and drying. Choose a site on a slope or high ground with good air drainage to reduce frost damage to the early spring blooms.
